ab_history.doc: Every recorded A/B comparison, oldest first.

arena_write.doc:
Write the map's arena file, which puts it in the game's map list with a name and briefing.

`longname` is the name players see. `keys` adds any other key the profile lists (for
ET: Legacy: `briefing`, `timelimit`, `axisRespawnTime`, `alliedRespawnTime`,
`mapposition_x`/`_y`, win texts, `type`); the map name and the profile's defaults are filled
in. Written beside the map's folder, where `pack_pk3` picks it up. Replaces an existing one.

asset_plan.doc:
Decide whether a feature should be a brush, a patch or a mesh.

The decision rule, in order: *does it block movement, block vis, or need cheap clean
collision?* → brush. *Is it axis-aligned architecture?* → brush. *Is it curved but simple?*
→ patch. *Everything else* → Blender.

That ordering is not arbitrary. Brushes are the only representation that seals a map and
blocks visibility, patches are never structural, and meshes are always non-structural — so
anything load-bearing has to be a brush regardless of how it looks.
asset_plan.signature: (blocks_movement: 'bool', blocks_visibility: 'bool', is_axis_aligned: 'bool', is_curved: 'bool', needs_clean_collision: 'bool' = False, is_organic: 'bool' = False) -> 'dict'

balance_report.doc:
Per-team traversal distance from each spawn group to each objective.

Reports path lengths over the walkable grid, the asymmetry between teams, and whether the map
is mirror-symmetric about its centre. Which classnames count as spawns and objectives comes
from the profile, so this works for any game with a profile.

Distances are walked, not straight-line — a 500-unit gap with a wall in it is not 500 units.
Uses the current unsaved map and staged script. `stance` selects stand/crouch/prone.

Profiles with reinforcement rules also report wave waits, estimated route times, active
spawn capacity and overlapping spawn boxes. `team_sizes` and `respawn_seconds` use the
profile's team IDs (red/blue in the shipped objective profile). `run_speed` overrides
units/second explicitly; crouch/prone times require it. No estimate models combat.

Optional `stages`: [{"name": "after gate", "spawn_entities": [3, 4],
"objective_entities": [8], "respawn_seconds": {"red": 20, "blue": 30}}]. These are
explicit spawn/objective selections on the SAME geometry snapshot, not script simulation.

`detail="summary"` (default): verdicts, counts, every error finding, and the rows that
need attention first; `omitted` names what was left out. `"full"` returns everything.
balance_report.signature: (cell: 'float' = 16, profile_id: 'str | None' = None, stance: 'str' = 'stand', stages: 'list[dict] | None' = None, team_sizes: 'dict[str, int] | None' = None, run_speed: 'float | None' = None, respawn_seconds: 'dict[str, float] | None' = None, detail: 'Detail' = 'summary') -> 'dict'

bench_run.doc:
Run the fitness suite and return the scores.

F1 (kernel correctness) is a **gate**, not a score: a run with it red has no score to compare,
whatever the other signals say. F4 skips without a compiler and F5 is a declarative proxy for
the natural-language-brief version; both say so in their output rather than reporting a number
they cannot justify.

Also reports whether the protected paths are unchanged. If they are not, treat every score as
meaningless: the ruler itself was edited.

blender_brief.doc:
Emit a numerically complete asset brief plus a ready-to-send Blender prompt.

`bounds` is `{"x": [lo, hi], "y": [...], "z": [...]}` in world units — normally the brush
volume the asset replaces.

The point is that the returned `prompt` leaves nothing to infer: dimensions, origin, budget,
material names, UV density, export axes and the collision decision are all decided here. A
brief that says "make it crate-sized" gets a crate of the wrong size.

The unit scale comes from the profile.
blender_brief.signature: (asset_id: 'str', purpose: 'str', bounds: 'dict', collision: 'str' = 'brush_hull', materials: 'list[dict] | None' = None, triangles: 'int | None' = None, silhouette_notes: 'str' = '', profile_id: 'str | None' = None) -> 'dict'

bot_playtest.doc:
Load a packaged map with its bot waypoints on a dedicated server, add bots, watch them.

`waypoints` is the file `bot_waypoints_write` staged (default: the open map's staged
file). With `scripts` (default) the map goals and map script staged beside it go too
(ET: Legacy `<map>_goals.gm`, `<map>.gm`), when present. The server runs for `seconds`
(10..600) in a throwaway game home, with a throwaway copy of the bot add-on's folder
(`addon_dir`, default the game install's own, for ET: Legacy `legacy/omni-bot`; it is
only read) whose nav folder holds just these files, so no stock or stale ones can stand
in for them. `bots` (1..32) bots join via the add-on's own command. `port` is the
server's UDP port (0 picks a free one).

With the scripts, `scripts` reports how many goals the add-on loaded, any goal or
script errors it logged, the map script's own messages (map-script debugging is
switched on in the throwaway folder only) with the goals each one switched, and per
goal spot the seconds a bot of its team stood on it, so a spot switched off by an
objective event can be seen emptied.

Reports what the add-on logged (`waypoints_loaded`, one count per map load; any
`load_errors`), per bot how far it travelled, how many distinct waypoints it passed
and the stances it was seen in (a read-only observer samples every 2 seconds), and the
game's own objective `events` (dynamite planted/defused, flags stolen, announcements,
the round ending). `ok` means the file loaded without errors and at least one bot
moved along the waypoints. Whether bots attempt an objective in a given run depends on
the add-on's goal choices and the fight; read `events`, and run longer for more.
`keep=true` retains the folders and names the logs. Needs the engine and game data.
`depends` lists other archives the map needs loaded with it, as for `engine_playtest`.
`nav_files` are more files for the add-on's nav folder beside the waypoints, such as the
map's bot script (for ET: Legacy Omni-bot, `<map>.gm`), named as the add-on wants them.

`ok` also needs the goals loaded and no goal or script error when scripts went in.
`detail="summary"` (default) leaves out the per-bot rows when more than 12 bots ran;
`"full"` always returns them.
bot_playtest.signature: (pk3: 'str', waypoints: 'str | None' = None, seconds: 'float' = 90, bots: 'int' = 6, addon_dir: 'str | None' = None, port: 'int' = 0, profile_id: 'str | None' = None, keep: 'bool' = False, scripts: 'bool' = True, depends: 'list[str] | None' = None, nav_files: 'list[str] | None' = None, detail: 'Detail' = 'summary') -> 'dict'

bot_waypoints_write.doc:
Seed the bot add-on's waypoint file for the open map from its stance navigation grids,
with the map goals (camping spots) and the map script that switches them.

For ET: Legacy this is an Omni-bot `.way` file (format version 9, read and written as
the add-on's own serializer does). Waypoints sit about `spacing` units apart (default
from the profile) on the walkable cells of the stand, crouch and prone grids (`cell`,
as in `route_report`); each is connected to its neighbours only where the straight line
between them is walkable, since bots steer straight between waypoints. Waypoints that
need crouch or prone carry that flag (bots press it while heading there). Brushes that
change state are seeded in every state and flagged for the add-on to test at runtime
(the profile's `bots:` section says which classes and flags):

- a door a player opens with the use key is passable, with a waypoint in the doorway
  carrying the door flag (bots press use heading for it) and, for a door `allowteams`
  limits to one team, that team's flags, so the other team never routes through it;
- a blown wall, a locked or scripted door, and a constructible that blocks a gap once
  built are walls: connections through them carry the wall flag, closed while solid;
- floor only a built constructible gives (a bridge deck) is no floor at round start:
  connections onto or across it carry the bridge flag, closed while nothing is under
  their midpoint, and are split at the deck's edges so that midpoint is over the deck.

Team spawns and every objective approach area get a named waypoint; parts of the map no
spawn connects to are dropped; walking off a ledge is a one-way connection. `doors`,
`constructibles` and the `bridge_*` / `door_*`
counts say what was gated.

Jumps and ladders (the profile's `bots.jumps` / `bots.ladders`): where walking between
two areas is impossible or a long detour, a ledge whose top is within the jump's rise
(swept with the standing box up its face) or a gap the box's ballistic arc clears from
every take-off point and at every speed the profile lists, gets a run-up waypoint, a
take-off waypoint flagged to jump (for ET: Legacy `JUMP`, small radius) and a ONE-WAY
connection to a landing waypoint (`JUMPLOW` on a ledge's). A brush whose shader has the
ladder surfaceparm gets a foot waypoint in front of its face and a top waypoint on the
floor at its top, both `CLIMB`, connected both ways. `jumps` and `ladders` list them
(a ladder without a reachable foot or top says why).

The add-on reads waypoints from its own folder, never from the map's pk3, so the file
is staged beside the map's folder under the profile's add-on layout (for ET: Legacy
`omni-bot/et/nav/<map>.way`), to be copied into the server's `omnibot_path`. Pass
`omnibot_path` to also write it there. Uses the current unsaved map.

`objectives` says, per objective, whether the graph reaches it from each team's spawn
waypoints. Objective goals (plant, build, capture) come from the game itself.

Beside the waypoints go two scripts the add-on runs at map load (ET: Legacy:
`<map>_goals.gm`, its map goals, and `<map>.gm`, the map script). With `auto_spots`
(default) spots are chosen from the geometry, each on a standing waypoint its team
reaches: per objective part a team defends (the thing to blow up, the flag it holds,
the item and, once stolen, its delivery place), up to two defend spots that see where
the other team uses it, ranked by how much of that team's shortest routes in they see
and facing it; per team, up to two snipe spots off the enemy's routes that see the most
of them at long range. `goals.spots[].why` says what each one sees. `spots` adds your
own: [{"type": "DEFEND", "team": "axis", "position": [x, y, z], "aim_at": [x, y, z]}],
with `yaw` (degrees) instead of `aim_at`, and optional `name`, `stance`,
`camp_time` [min, max] seconds and `objective` (its spots' on/off follows that
objective's); positions snap to the nearest walkable floor. Types are the profile's
(DEFEND, ATTACK, CAMP, SNIPE, MOBILEMG42, MOBILEMORTAR; SNIPE is for sniper rifles).

The map script hooks each objective's events by the trigger names the game sends:
the game's own "Planted at <track>." / "Defused at <track>." and the announcements in
the map's script (read from the staged script, so edited texts still match). Each
hook switches its objective's spots per team: a destroyed objective's defenders stand
down, a built one is defended, a captured flag changes defenders, a stolen item sends
them to its delivery place. `goals.triggers` lists them; `goals.not_hooked` names
events the map's script gives no text for (add a wm_announce there). Both scripts are
read back before anything is written.
`bot_playtest` loads all three in the engine with bots and reports what they did.

`detail="summary"` (default) leaves out the per-pin rows and why each spot was chosen;
`"full"` returns them.
bot_waypoints_write.signature: (cell: 'float' = 16, spacing: 'float | None' = None, omnibot_path: 'str | None' = None, spots: 'list[dict] | None' = None, auto_spots: 'bool' = True, detail: 'Detail' = 'summary') -> 'dict'

brush_geometry.doc:
Exact vertices and derived properties of one brush.

Vertices are computed with exact integer arithmetic. When a brush cannot be evaluated
exactly — off-grid plane points, too few faces — this reports `usable: false` with a
reason rather than returning approximate numbers that look authoritative.

brush_set_detail.doc:
Mark existing brushes detail (or structural again with `detail=false`).

A detail brush still blocks players and shots but no longer splits the vis tree, which is
the biggest lever on vis cost: trim, pillars, props and anything that does not seal the map
should be detail. `brushes` is a list of `[entity, primitive]` pairs, or the findings
`structural_audit` returns (each carries its entity and primitive), passed straight in.

Every brush is checked before any is changed; a patch or a missing primitive refuses the
whole call. Nothing reaches disk until `map_save`. New geometry can be made detail as it is
built: `solid_commit(textures={"detail": true, ...})`.

bsp_entity_diff.doc:
Compare a compiled BSP's entity lump against the source `.map`.

Entities can be dropped silently at compile time — the editor's writer discards empty
group entities and q3map2 drops what it cannot place — so a count that quietly changed is
a real bug this catches.

bsp_report.doc:
Read a compiled BSP's structure from an unpacked `-json` lump directory.

Produce the directory with `task_run("bsp:json-unpack", [path_to_bsp])`.

Reports surfaces per shader (which shader is eating draw calls), surface types, lightmap
coverage, unreferenced shaders, and headroom. Headroom comes in two parts and the
distinction matters: **compiler limits** are read from this fork's source and are real,
but most of the classic Quake 3 ceilings were removed upstream, so there is nothing to
report for them. **Engine limits** come from the profile and are what decide whether the
map loads at all — a map can compile cleanly and still be rejected in game.

commandmap_make.doc:
Draw the command map and tell the game where it lies.

Sets the worldspawn's map coordinates to a square around the map (plus `margin`), draws a
top-down section of the map into exactly that square - roofs cut away above `cut_height`,
walls in a dark section colour - and writes the image and the shaders the game draws it
with, beside the map's folder. Default `cut_height`: a standing player's height above the
highest spawn. Save the map afterwards: the coordinates are worldspawn keys.

compile_ab.doc:
Compile two variants and diff the numbers that matter.

Reports per-stage wall time, draw surface count, leaf count, brush count and BSP size for each,
and appends a row to `bench/ab-history.jsonl` so regressions stay visible over the life of a
project rather than being rediscovered.

This is how a structural_audit suggestion gets *confirmed* rather than assumed: apply it to a
copy, compile both, and read the portal delta.

compile_map.doc:
Compile a map with q3map2.

Presets (§6.1): `draft` geometry-only seconds-long check, `iterate` playable test build,
`quality` review build, `final` release build.

On a WSL host where q3map2 is a Windows binary, the wrapper stages the map onto the
Windows filesystem and copies artefacts back to `out/` — paths are handled for you.

With no path (or the open map's path), compile a snapshot of the current unsaved map
and staged companions. The result identifies that revision and its retained build folder.

engine_playtest.doc:
Exercise a packaged map with real player controls and fresh state assertions.

Read `nrc://playtest/{profile_id}` for the scenario schema, supported inputs and fields.
A scenario has `watch` names and ordered `steps`: join, position, aim, weapon, hold,
wait, assert or screenshot. Each `until` is a list of predicates that must all match
one fresh observation, e.g. {"scope":"player","field":"alive","value":true}.
Joins wait for a living player; holds release on success, timeout and failure.

`position` and `aim` are explicit test setup; `aim` takes angles, or `at` a point or a
vector field of the latest observation (e.g. where a dynamite charge landed). Other
actions use ordinary controls; the profile observer reads state without changing
entities or executing scripts. `objective_playtests` writes scenarios for a map's
objectives.
Steps have bounded timeouts, with an overall limit of 600 seconds. An isolated game
home, commands, observations, screenshots and result.json are retained even on failure.
This tests a single client, not multiplayer balance. Requires a supported profile,
POSIX console transport, game data and a display (or Xvfb).

Returns the JSON receipt and, by default, the last three screenshot image blocks.
`include_images=false` returns just the JSON receipt; all image paths remain recorded.
`depends` lists other archives the map needs loaded with it (a map built on another
map's textures and models, packed with `pack_pk3(depends=...)`).

`detail="summary"` (default) gives passing steps as verdicts and failed steps in full;
`"full"` adds every observation, the scenario echo and the command line.
engine_playtest.signature: (pk3: 'str', scenario: 'dict', profile_id: 'str | None' = None, timeout_seconds: 'float' = 180, include_images: 'bool' = True, depends: 'list[str] | None' = None, detail: 'Detail' = 'summary') -> 'list'

entities_place.doc:
Add many point entities in one call, all or none: lights, spawns, markers.

Each item is `{"classname": ..., "origin": [x, y, z], "keys": {...}}`, checked exactly as
`entity_place` checks one. Every item is checked before any is added, so a refusal names
the item (`entities[3]: ...`) and changes nothing.

The reply is compact: the new indices, in the order given, and each distinct note once
with the items it applies to. Ten lights with the same key produce one note, not ten.
Read the notes: a key the profile does not declare is written anyway and does nothing
in game if it is misspelt. For team spawns with their region marker, `spawn_cluster`
also finds the standing positions. Nothing reaches disk until `map_save`.

entity_place.doc:
Add a point entity to the open map: a spawn, a script or objective marker, a light.

`keys` are written after `classname` and `origin`, in the order given. A number becomes
its shortest spelling and a list of numbers a space-separated vector, so
`{"angles": [0, 90, 0]}` writes `"angles" "0 90 0"`.

The classname and keys are checked against the active profile and anything it does not
declare comes back in `notes` — written anyway, because profiles are incomplete, but a
misspelt key is silent in game, so read them. `profile_summary` and `nrc://profile/{id}`
list what the profile knows. The origin is written as given, never snapped; one off the
grid (default: the session's) is noted, as the brush tools count off-grid vertices.

A classname the profile declares as a brush entity — a door, a trigger — is refused: build
its brushes with `solid_commit` and `target_classname`, then give it keys with
`entity_set_keys`. Nothing reaches disk until `map_save`. To add several entities, use
`entities_place`: one call, all or none.
entity_place.signature: (classname: 'str', origin: 'list[float]', keys: 'dict[str, str | float | list[float]] | None' = None, grid: 'int | None' = None) -> 'dict'

entity_remove_keys.doc:
Remove keys from any entity, every copy of each.

`entity` is the index `query_entities` reports. A key the entity does not have is listed
in `absent` rather than refused, so the call is safe to repeat. `classname` cannot be
removed: change it with `entity_set_keys` instead. Nothing reaches disk until `map_save`.

entity_set_keys.doc:
Set keys on any entity — a point entity, a brush entity or the worldspawn.

`entity` is the index `query_entities` reports; worldspawn is normally 0. An existing key
keeps its position and gets the new value; a new key is appended. Values are spelt as in
`entity_place`. Changing `classname` is allowed, except on the worldspawn or into a
second one.

The previous value of every key comes back in `changed`, because this overwrites. If the
entity carried a key twice, the later copy is what the engine reads, so it is removed and
reported in `duplicates_removed`. Keys and values the profile does not declare for the
classname come back in `notes`, as in `entity_place`.

Every key is checked before any is written, so a refusal changes nothing. Nothing
reaches disk until `map_save`.

hint_suggest.doc:
Propose hint brush planes from a compiled portal file.

Needs a `.prt`, which `-vis -saveprt` writes: compile with the `final` preset, or run
`task_run("compile:final", [map])`.

Each suggestion names the leaf, its portal count and a proposed splitting plane, with a
predicted before/after — predicted, because confirming it needs another `-vis` run.

leak_trace.doc:
Read a leak pointfile and report the path out of the map.

q3map2 writes a `.lin` beside the map when the world is not sealed. The path runs from the
void inwards: the first point is outside the map, the last is the origin of the entity that
leaked (leakfile.cpp:80-107), and the hull is open where the path crosses it.

With a map open and the active profile describing what seals (`sealing:`), the findings also
name likely causes on the path: a brush that looks solid but has a side whose shader is
translucent to the compiler (`alphashadow`, `trans`, clip and the like make the whole brush
detail and non-opaque), detail brushes, and model entities, which never seal. Shaders are
looked up in the base game (with the game path set) and the map's own scripts.

Defaults to the most recent session build's `.lin`, with that build's revision.
Without a session build, checks beside the open map. Explicit paths remain supported.

levelshot_make.doc:
Render the levelshot - the picture shown while the map loads and in the server browser.

Taken from a standing player's eyes at the floor `position`, looking along `yaw_deg`
(0 = +X, 90 = +Y), at the profile's preferred size. Written beside the map's folder.

lighting_report.doc:
What lights the map, and where players stand far from any light.

Read the way q3map2 reads it: an entity whose classname starts with `light` is a light, at
intensity 300 unless its `light`/`_light` key says otherwise (light.cpp:330, :439-442);
the worldspawn's `_ambient` (or `ambient`) lights everything evenly, and `_minlight` sets a
floor (light.cpp:1946, :1959). A map with none of these compiles black. Sky shaders that
emit light are not read here.

`reach` is a heuristic, not q3map2's falloff: walkable areas farther than that from every
light are listed as possibly dim. With ambient or minimum light set they are lit anyway.

map_checkpoint.doc:
Remember the current geometry and staged companions under a name, without saving.

Use map_restore to undo back to it. Checkpoints last until a save or another map is opened.

map_mirror.doc:
Mirror the open map across the plane `axis = at`: geometry, entities, facings.

Every brush and patch is reflected with its planes kept outward (the kernel swaps the
plane points' order, which a reflection otherwise turns inside out), its texture mapping
rewritten so the surface shows the mirror image of the original, and its patch grid
reordered so it keeps facing out. Then the entity keys the profile names (`mirror:` in
`nrc://profile/{id}`; ET: Legacy: `origin`, `angle`, `angles`, the command map corners)
are reflected: a facing `a` along x becomes `180 - a` (along y, `-a`), `angles`
`p y r` becomes `p 180-y -r` (`p -y -r`), and doors that swing are made to swing the
mirrored way. Special yaw values (ET: -1 up, -2 down) stay.

`vehicles` names (targetname or scriptname) brush entities the game turns to face their
direction of travel, such as an escort truck on a spline and the triggers riding on it.
Mirrored in place, their local "forward" would point backwards; each is given a half
turn about its own origin instead, so it drives forward along the mirrored path and is
the mirror image of itself across its own length.

What it cannot mirror, it reports: raw primitive blocks the kernel keeps as text, and
models (`misc_model` and the like), which turn to the mirrored facing but are drawn
unmirrored. A map script is not touched; coordinates or angles written in it (rotation
targets, `faceangles`) need mirroring by hand. Nothing reaches disk until `map_save`.

map_new.doc:
Create an empty `.map` holding only a worldspawn, and open it.

The start of a map built from nothing: then `solid_commit` for geometry, `entity_place`
for point entities, `map_save` to write. An existing file is never overwritten — open it
with `map_open` instead. Missing parent folders are created. A generated-solid sidecar
left beside the path by an earlier map describes none of this one's brushes: it is not
adopted, and `map_save` replaces it.

Args:
    path: where to create it, ending in `.map`. Relative paths resolve against the repo root.
    grid: authoring grid, as for `map_open`.
    discard_unsaved: as for `map_open`.

map_open.doc:
Open a `.map` file for analysis.

Refused while the open map has edits or staged files `map_save` has not written, which
opening another map would throw away; save them first, or pass `discard_unsaved`.

Args:
    path: path to the `.map`. Relative paths resolve against the repo root.
    grid: authoring grid that off-grid geometry is measured against.
    discard_unsaved: open anyway, dropping the open map's unsaved work.

Returns a summary plus a round-trip check. If `round_trip.identical` is false, treat
every later answer about this map with suspicion and report it — that is the §3.2 gate
failing on a real file, which is a kernel bug worth fixing before anything else.

map_restore.doc:
Restore geometry and staged companions from map_checkpoint; disk is untouched.

Save to persist the restored state. Saving clears checkpoints; this undoes staged edits.

map_save.doc:
Write the open map back to disk, if it is safe to.

Staged script and generated-solid sidecars are saved with the map. Three gates apply.

**The file.** If the kernel could not reproduce the bytes it *loaded*, it misunderstands
something in this file and writing would silently discard it. That check is taken at
`map_open` and it is the one enforced here. A difference introduced since then is your
edit, not a kernel failure, and does not block the write.

**The map.** The write is compared against the open map's file on disk (for a Save As,
the file it was opened from: the destination must not exist yet), and refused if it
destroys playable space — an interior floor sealed off, or a surface you can now
stand on top of a clip volume. Both are silent in every other check: the map still
compiles, still seals, still validates, and is unplayable. See `playable_space_diff` for
the same report on its own.

**Other edits.** Refuse if a destination changed on disk since this session read it.
All writes are prepared before replacing files; a write failure rolls replacements back.
A successful save clears checkpoints. Individual replacements are atomic, but this is
not a filesystem-wide transaction across multiple files.

The comparison costs a second or two on a city-sized map. If it cannot be made at all —
a map too large to voxelize, or one with no evaluable brush — the write proceeds and
says so, because a check that cannot run has not found anything.

Args:
    path: destination. Defaults to the open map. Save As requires a new destination,
        copies known companions and makes the new path current.
    allow_non_identical: write even though the map did not round-trip when it was opened.
    check_playable_space: run the before/after comparison. Off skips it entirely.
    acknowledge_regression: write anyway despite a playable-space error. Use it when you
        meant to remove that space.
map_save.signature: (path: 'str | None' = None, allow_non_identical: 'bool' = False, check_playable_space: 'bool' = True, acknowledge_regression: 'bool' = False) -> 'dict'

map_stats.doc:
Statistics for the open map: counts, bounds, shader histogram, grid alignment.

`structural_brushes` vs `detail_brushes` is the split that matters most for vis
performance (§6.1): structural brushes block visibility and are expensive, detail
brushes do not.

model_import.doc:
Validate an exported mesh against the brief that asked for it.

Checks scale, fit, origin, triangle budget, material names, UVs and structure. The scale
check comes first and names the likely cause: a mesh 1/39.37 of the requested size is the
metres-exported-as-units mistake, and saying so is far more useful than reporting the raw
numbers.

model_make_clip.doc:
Fit a convex collision hull to a mesh, returned as Solid IR.

The hull is a k-DOP: the tightest intersection of half-spaces with `k` fixed normals that
contains every vertex, pushed outward to the grid so it never cuts into the visual: simple,
predictable collision rather than an exact fit.

`kind` selects the clip shader from the profile: `player` for movement only, `weapon` to stop
bullets where the visual has gaps, `both` for solid.

Returns IR rather than brushes, so preview it with `solid_preview` and look at it against the
model before committing. A hull noticeably larger than the visual is what players report as
an invisible wall.
model_make_clip.signature: (path: 'str', origin: 'list[float] | None' = None, scale: 'float' = 1.0, k: 'int' = 14, grid: 'int' = 1, kind: 'str' = 'player', profile_id: 'str | None' = None) -> 'dict'

model_place.doc:
Add a model-placing entity to the open map.

This **modifies the open map**. `model_place_plan` takes the same arguments and returns
the keys without touching anything, which is the one to call while you are still deciding.

Nothing reaches disk until `map_save`.
model_place.signature: (model_path: 'str', origin: 'list[float]', angles: 'list[float] | None' = None, scale: 'float | None' = None, lightmap_scale: 'float | None' = None, remap: 'dict | None' = None, profile_id: 'str | None' = None) -> 'dict'

model_place_plan.doc:
Build the entity that *would* place a model, without touching the map.

Every key name comes from the profile: the model entity's classname, the scale keys, the
remap prefix. Negative scale is supported by this compiler and is the cheapest way to mirror
a prop.

Check the keys here, then call `model_place` to add them. This tool changes nothing.
model_place_plan.signature: (model_path: 'str', origin: 'list[float]', angles: 'list[float] | None' = None, scale: 'float | None' = None, lightmap_scale: 'float | None' = None, remap: 'dict | None' = None, profile_id: 'str | None' = None) -> 'dict'

movement_check.doc:
Check clearances against the profile's movement constants.

Standing headroom, crouch headroom, step height, doorway widths. Every finding names the
constant it used and that constant's confidence, and **anything derived from an unverified
constant is reported as info, never an error**.

`detail` as in `balance_report`.

navgrid_stats.doc:
Build the walkable grid and report its size and coverage.

A cell is walkable when it is empty, the cell below is solid, and there is at least the
profile's standing height of clear space above it — so the grid is the space a player could
actually occupy, not merely the empty space.

This is a **voxel approximation, not compiled AAS**. It is good enough for distances and
reachability and will disagree with the engine at the margins. Everything else here is built on
it, so run this first to see whether the map is tractable at the cell size you want.

`stance` selects stand, crouch or prone; player-width clearance is included. Prone
checks use the profile body box only, not a full turning/legs simulation.

Read `reachable_share` before the rest: below 1.0, some standable floor cannot be reached
from the largest region, and every distance the other reports derive is measured across a
space the player cannot actually cross.

objdata_write.doc:
Write the descriptions players read in the limbo menu: the map's, and each objective's.

`descriptions` maps a team (for ET: Legacy `axis`, `allied`, `neutral`) to its text;
`objectives` maps a team to a list of texts, numbered in order from 1, matching the
objective numbers the map script uses. Replaces an existing file.

objective_place.doc:
Build a whole objective in one call: its trigger, the objective entities, keys and script.

The kinds are the profile's (`objectives:` in `nrc://profile/{id}`, which describes each);
for ET: Legacy:

- `dynamite`: the other team blows it up. `team` owns and defends it.
- `constructible`: `team`'s engineers build it; the other team can blow it up once built.
- `command_post`: the stock command post. Built, it shortens its team's charge times and
  reports landmines to it; destroyed, that stops. `team` is `neutral` (either team builds
  it, one at a time), `axis` or `allies` (only that team builds it).
- `checkpoint`: a forward spawn flag both teams capture. `team` holds it, and its spawns,
  at the start.
- `checkpoint_one_way`: the same, but only the other team can raise its flag. `team` can
  still knock that flag down, and that hands the spawns back (the engine's rule).
- `escort`: a vehicle `team` escorts along `path` (the `start` from `path_place`). It moves
  while `team` players stand in `trigger`, stops at the next path point a couple of seconds
  after they leave, and runs `trigger arrived` on `name` at the end. Not damageable.
- `steal`: an item the other team steals from `team` and carries into `trigger`, which
  runs `death` on `<name>_deliver`; `objective` is where it lies.

`objective` and `trigger` are boxes `{"min": [...], "max": [...]}` or Solid IR trees, for
the kinds that have them: the objective's own brushes (a vehicle as it stands at the path's
first point), and the volume players stand in - to see "You are near <track>" and plant or
build, to escort, or to deliver. Where the objective is a point entity (a stolen item),
`objective` may also be `{"origin": [x, y, z]}`. Make the trigger enclose the objective
with room to stand. `texture` goes on the objective's brushes.

`points` places point entities by role, for the kinds that have them:
`{"flag": [x, y, z], "spawns": [[x, y, z], {"origin": [x, y, z], "angle": 90}, ...]}`.
For a checkpoint, `flag` is the foot of the flagpole, and the spawn region marker named
`track` goes there too. Each of `spawns` gets one spawn for each team, linked to the flag:
the holder's start active, and a capture hands them to the capturing team. Spawns are
optional; place them later with the targetname given under `links`.

`options` sets a kind's tunables, such as an escort's `speed` or a stolen item's `model`;
the profile lists them with their defaults.

The links the engine needs are made for you - triggers target what they work, a dynamite
objective carries its weapon class, a vehicle carries the origin it turns about - and the
script gets the objective's events, which you can extend with `script_set_event`. Nothing
in the map reaches disk until `map_save`; the script is staged with it.
objective_place.signature: (kind: 'str', name: 'str', track: 'str', team: 'str', objective: 'dict | None' = None, trigger: 'dict | None' = None, texture: 'str' = '', points: 'dict | None' = None, path: 'str' = '', options: 'dict[str, str | float] | None' = None) -> 'dict'

objective_playtests.doc:
Write an `engine_playtest` scenario that plays every objective in the open map.

Objectives are recognised from the map's entities and script, not from how they were
made: each kind in the profile's `objectives:` (`nrc://profile/{id}`) carries a
`playtest:` template that says how to find one, which team and class play it, what they
do, and which observation proves it worked. For ET: Legacy: dynamite is planted, armed and
destroys the objective; a constructible or command post is built with pliers; a checkpoint
is captured and retaken, proved by where the attackers respawn; an escort vehicle is
followed to the end of its path and checked to stop without its escort; a stolen item is
picked up and delivered. When the objective's script events lead to a round end, the test
also waits for intermission and the winner its script sets.

Every standing position is floor the player box rests on with headroom, on the walkable
grid, inside the right volume and clear of the objective's brushes, and joined to one of
the team's spawns by a walkable route (`standing[].route`). `cell` is that grid's size.

`runs` are what to pass to `engine_playtest`: `scenario` and `timeout_seconds` each. A test
that ends the round closes its run, so a map with two winning objectives needs two runs.
`tests` lists each objective's test on its own, with what it `proves`; `skipped` lists the
objectives (and objective entities) no test could be made for, and why. `objective` limits
this to one objective, by name. Nothing is changed or launched; pack the map first.
objective_playtests.signature: (objective: 'str | None' = None, cell: 'float' = 16, profile_id: 'str | None' = None) -> 'dict'

pack_pk3.doc:
Build a release archive for a compiled BSP with `q3map2 -pk3` (§6.4).

The packer's own naming is the first oracle: a `_FAILEDpack.pk3` means it could not find
a resource the BSP references. Each name it missed is then checked again, because the
packer cannot read shaders defined with `implicitMap` and reports them missing although the
base game ships them. A name counts as found when the base game supplies it, the map's own
shader script defines it (script and images are packed), a file of that name sits beside
the map, the profile lists it under `packaging.allowed_missing` (stock assets the base game
never shipped), or it matches `ignore`: exact names or shell patterns such as
`sound/world/*`, for resources you know the game does without. If all are found the
package is `_autopacked.pk3`; whatever is left is in `not_found` and the pack still fails.
`packer_not_found` is the packer's own list, `accounted_for` and `allowed_missing` say what
became of each.

The archive is then fixed up from the active profile: companion files and the arena that
sit beside the map are added, with the sound files its speaker and sound scripts name,
files the base game already ships are dropped, and it is written next to the folder that
holds `maps/`, never into the game install.

`depends` lists other archives the map is played alongside, whose textures, models and
sounds it uses (a map built on another map's assets): what they hold counts as found and
is not copied in. Load them with the package, e.g. `engine_playtest(depends=...)`. For the
compiler to see them, keep them beside the folder that holds `maps/`.

`detail="summary"` (default) keeps `not_found` and `allowed_missing` whole and caps the
other lists; `"full"` adds the packer's console tail and every row.
pack_pk3.signature: (bsp: 'str', complevel: 'int | None' = None, png: 'bool' = False, ignore: 'list[str] | None' = None, depends: 'list[str] | None' = None, detail: 'Detail' = 'summary') -> 'dict'

patch_commit.doc:
Add a curved surface - brushes cannot curve, so the engine draws curves from patches.

Kinds:
  - `cylinder`: a column or pipe along `axis` (`x`, `y`, or default `z`). `centre` is
    the circle's centre at the starting end; `length` extends along the positive axis.
  - `arch`: a half-round vault spanning a doorway or corridor, running along `axis`
    (`x` or `y`). `centre` is the middle of the circle at one end, on the springing line;
    `length` is the depth along the axis.
  - `bevel`: a quarter-round for softening a corner, vertical by default. `start_deg`
    (0, 90, 180, 270) picks the quarter; `centre`, `length`, and `axis` as for a cylinder.

`facing` is the side that is drawn: `out` (default for cylinder and bevel) or `in` (default
for an arch, seen from below); the engine collides with that same side. Patches do not
seal the map. Player collision depends on the shader's contents. The engine collides with
a coarse polygon, not the drawn curve: each quarter-circle is one straight chord until its
midpoint would sit 16 units or more off the curve (radius 45.3 and up), so a 24-radius pipe
collides as a 45-degree diamond. The movement analysis uses the same polygon. The patch
joins the worldspawn, a new entity of any other `target_classname`, or the entity
`target_entity` names, as for `solid_commit`. Nothing reaches disk until `map_save`.
patch_commit.signature: (kind: 'str', centre: 'list[float]', radius: 'float', length: 'float', shader: 'str', axis: 'str' = 'z', facing: 'str | None' = None, start_deg: 'float' = 0.0, target_classname: 'str' = 'worldspawn', new_entity: 'bool' = False, target_entity: 'int | None' = None, label: 'str | None' = None) -> 'dict'

path_place.doc:
Lay a path for a mover to follow: a chain of named path points, straight or curved.

`points` are where the mover's origin travels, in order, at least two: each `[x, y, z]`,
or `{"at": [x, y, z], "controls": [[x, y, z], ...]}` to bend the segment that leaves that
point into a curve pulled towards its control points (the profile says how many a segment
may have; ET: Legacy takes four). The last point has no segment, so no controls.

The points are named `<name>_0`, `<name>_1`, ... and each names the next, as the engine
links them; control points are `<name>_<i>_c<j>`. The first point's name comes back as
`start`: pass it to `objective_place(path=...)`. A mover stops only at points, so for a
vehicle that should halt soon after its escort leaves, keep segments short:
`max_segment` splits every straight segment longer than that into equal ones.

For an escort vehicle, put the points at the height of the vehicle's middle and the first
one inside the vehicle where it starts: the vehicle keeps its offset from the point it
travels with, and turns to face along each segment. Nothing reaches disk until `map_save`.

playable_space_diff.doc:
Compare the space a player can stand in, between two versions of a map.

This is the check that no amount of validating, compiling or leak-testing performs: all
of those pass on a map whose streets have been filled with clip. Only a before/after
comparison sees it.

Two findings are errors rather than observations, because neither has a legitimate form:

- `PLAYSPACE_INTERIOR_SEALED` — floor that had a ceiling over it is no longer standable.
  A roof is sky-exposed by definition, so this is the inside of the map being closed off.
- `PLAYSPACE_CLIP_SURFACE_WALKABLE` — you can now stand on top of a clip volume. Clip
  stops the player, so capping something with clip does not remove the surface, it
  raises it.

Args:
    before: the earlier map.
    after: the later map. Defaults to the map open in this session, including edits that
        have not been written yet — which is how you check a change before committing it.
    cell: voxel size. Coarser is faster and still comparable; both sides use the same one.
    profile_id: game profile supplying the movement constants and clip shader names.
playable_space_diff.signature: (before: 'str', after: 'str | None' = None, cell: 'float' = 32.0, profile_id: 'str | None' = None) -> 'dict'

pr_plan_status.doc:
Regenerate and summarize the upstream contribution plan.

Every number is measured, not asserted. The three criteria that cannot be met from here — never
compiled, no usage telemetry, no maintainer asked — are reported as unmet rather than glossed.
Never invent the telemetry: an RPC method with no real-session usage is cut before submission.

profile_summary.doc:
What the active game profile knows, and how much of it is verified.

The profile is the only game-specific layer (§7.4). Anything marked `unverified` came
from documentation rather than a shipped gamepack and must not be treated as a hard
rule.

query_entities.doc:
Entities in the open map, optionally filtered by classname.

Keys come back as ordered pairs rather than a mapping, because key order is meaningful
in a `.map` and duplicate keys occur in real files.

render_camera.doc:
Render a perspective view, or one of the front/side orthographic views.

Args:
    eye: camera position. Omit for an automatic three-quarter framing of the whole map.
    target: what to look at. Defaults to the centre of the geometry.
    view: `perspective`, `front` or `side`.
    hide_invisible: skip caulk, nodraw, clip and trigger surfaces. On by default because a
        sealed map is wrapped in such a shell, and a perspective view of the shell shows
        nothing useful.
render_camera.signature: (eye: 'list[float] | None' = None, target: 'list[float] | None' = None, fov_deg: 'float' = 55.0, overlay: 'str' = 'shaded', width: 'int' = 1000, height: 'int' = 800, hide_invisible: 'bool' = True, view: 'str' = 'perspective') -> 'list'

render_contact_sheet.doc:
Render three orthographic views plus a perspective view in one image.

This is the default way to look at geometry: one call, one image, and a shape that three
orthographic views plus a perspective view make unambiguous. Panels clockwise from
top-left are top (XY), front (XZ), side (YZ), perspective.

render_player_eye.doc:
Render the view a standing player would have from a floor position.

Args:
    position: floor point to stand on, `[x, y, z]`.
    yaw_deg: facing, degrees counter-clockwise from +X.
    eye_height: height above `position`. Omit to read the verified standing height from
        the active game profile.

Position `z` should be the floor, not the eye. If the result looks empty, the point is
probably inside solid geometry or outside the map.
render_player_eye.signature: (position: 'list[float]', yaw_deg: 'float' = 0.0, fov_deg: 'float' = 90.0, width: 'int' = 900, height: 'int' = 700, eye_height: 'float | None' = None) -> 'list'

render_topdown.doc:
Render a top-down (XY) view of the open map.

Orthographic views render as backface-culled wireframe, which gives a readable
architectural floor plan. A *solid* top-down of a sealed map shows only the underside of
its sky brush — one flat rectangle — so pass `solid=True` only when you know the geometry
is open.

Args:
    overlay: `shaded`, `structural` (colour by structural/detail/entity/patch),
        `caulk` (highlight surfaces not drawn in game), or `off_grid` (mark bad vertices).
    grid: grid that off-grid vertices are measured against. Defaults to the session grid.
    grid_spacing: world-unit spacing of the drawn grid; 0 disables it.
    solid: fill faces instead of drawing wireframe.
render_topdown.signature: (overlay: 'str' = 'shaded', width: 'int' = 1000, height: 'int' = 800, grid: 'int | None' = None, grid_spacing: 'float' = 64.0, solid: 'bool' = False) -> 'list'

repack_analyze.doc:
List every resource a compiled BSP references, via `q3map2 -repack -analyze`.

Parsed from the compiler's own dump rather than traced independently — the compiler's view
of what a BSP needs is the one that decides whether the map works.

route_render.doc:
Draw a route over a top-down geometry view, coloured by stance with change markers.

Parameters and planning limitations match `route_report`. The PNG and JSON witness
use the same immutable current-map snapshot and revision. All floors project onto XY:
use the witness's Z coordinates to distinguish overlapping levels. Width/height must
be integers from 256 to 2048. An unsuccessful search still returns map geometry and
the reason; it never draws an invented connection. `detail` as in `route_report`.
route_render.signature: (start: 'list[float] | None' = None, end: 'list[float] | None' = None, start_entity: 'int | None' = None, end_entity: 'int | None' = None, stance: 'str' = 'mixed', cell: 'float' = 16, profile_id: 'str | None' = None, start_stance: 'str | None' = None, end_stance: 'str | None' = None, stance_costs: 'dict[str, float] | None' = None, transition_cost: 'float' = 32, max_nodes: 'int' = 100000, snap_radius: 'float | None' = None, width: 'int' = 1000, height: 'int' = 800, detail: 'Detail' = 'summary') -> 'list'

route_report.doc:
Find a directed route with a geometric witness and explicit stance changes.

Give exactly one of `start` (floor XYZ) / `start_entity`, and one of `end` /
`end_entity`. Spawn origins snap to floor; brush objectives use their approach area.
Linked objective entities resolve to the same interaction area. Snap displacement is
reported separately and excluded from route distance.

`stance` is stand/crouch/prone or `mixed` (all stances described by the profile).
Mixed routes start and end standing by default. `start_stance`/`end_stance` may select
a stance or `any`. Stance changes occur only where both body boxes fit on the same cell.

Minimized cost is distance times a stance weight plus `transition_cost` per change.
Defaults are stand=1, crouch=1.5, prone=2 and transition=32 weighted world units.
These are explicit planning preferences, NOT speeds or seconds. Override them with
`stance_costs`. Path vertices retain every corner and transition; only collinear
interior vertices are omitted. Step/drop witnesses follow their checked lift/horizontal/
lower sweep legs, and distance measures those legs. Width and floor separation are checked.

Uses the current unsaved map. This is voxel planning: no jumping, animation, prone
legs/turning or script-state simulation. Patches collide as the engine's own facets
(coarser than the drawn curve). `max_nodes` (1..250000) bounds search; exhaustion
returns reachable=null rather than claiming no route.
`route_render` draws the same report over the map geometry.

`detail="summary"` (default) omits the model caveats, per-grid constants and the
per-vertex `path` (`segments` holds the same vertices); `"full"` returns everything.

Link checks: pass `links` (instead of start/end) to check up to 20000 links in one call,
each `[start, end]` or `{"start", "end", "stance"}` (a link's own stance overrides
`stance`). Every link is the same search as a single route; the grid's edges are
learned once and shared, so thousands of short waypoint links are cheap. Rows come back
in order with index, status (found, unreachable, budget_exhausted, no_endpoint,
exceeds_max_detour), distance, cost, straight_line, detour_ratio and the snapped ends;
`segments`/`transitions` only with `detail="full"`.

`max_detour` (single route or links) bounds the search: no route costing more than
max_detour x the straight line (x the cheapest stance weight) is looked for, so a failed
short link explores only the ellipse around it. A route inside the bound is the same
answer as without it; one outside reports `exceeds_max_detour`. Needs position endpoints.
route_report.signature: (start: 'list[float] | None' = None, end: 'list[float] | None' = None, start_entity: 'int | None' = None, end_entity: 'int | None' = None, stance: 'str' = 'mixed', cell: 'float' = 16, profile_id: 'str | None' = None, start_stance: 'str | None' = None, end_stance: 'str | None' = None, stance_costs: 'dict[str, float] | None' = None, transition_cost: 'float' = 32, max_nodes: 'int' = 100000, snap_radius: 'float | None' = None, links: 'list | None' = None, max_detour: 'float | None' = None, detail: 'Detail' = 'summary') -> 'dict'

script_remove.doc:
Remove one event from a block of the open map's script, or the whole block.

Without `event`, the whole block goes, and with it every later block of the same name:
only the first of a name runs, so removing it alone would make a forgotten copy run
instead. `removed_blocks` says how many went. Everything else in the file is left as it
was. The script is staged until `map_save`.
script_remove.signature: (block: 'str', event: 'str | None' = None, params: 'list[str] | None' = None) -> 'dict'

script_set_event.doc:
Set one event's actions in a block of the open map's script, creating what is missing.

`actions` are the event's lines in order, each one action with its arguments, e.g.
`["wait 50", "setautospawn "Axis Bunker" 0"]`. They replace the event's current actions;
the event, its block and the script file are created if they do not exist. `params` follow
the event name, as in `trigger open`. Everything else in the file - comments, layout,
line endings, other blocks, every byte - is left exactly as it was; setting the actions an
event already has changes nothing (`did: unchanged`).

Refused before anything is staged: an event or action the profile does not list, and a
line the engine would read differently from how it looks - a comment, an open quote, an
empty `""`, a brace among an action's arguments, text past ASCII outside quotes. The edited
script is parsed again and must read exactly as asked. Staged, then reported in
`findings`: references that resolve to nothing yet, since the entity may be placed next.
`map_save` saves the script with the map and checks for external changes.

script_show.doc:
The open map's script: its blocks and events, which entities run each block, and findings.

For a game whose maps carry a script beside the `.map` (the profile's `mapscript:`). A block
with an empty `runs_for_entities` never runs: no entity names it. The findings are the same
ones `validate_profile` reports for the script. Every action is shown as a line
`script_set_event` takes back as it is.

selfdev_protected.doc:
List the paths self-modification may never touch, and verify their hash pins.

Read-only, and available whether or not self-dev is enabled: knowing what is frozen is useful
on its own.

shader_audit.doc:
Audit shader references against the shader scripts on disk.

Reports shaders the map references but nothing defines, shaders defined but never used,
shaders shadowing a base-game path — a classic cause of "works for me, broken on the server" —
and the watercaulk trap, where a visible surface's shader draws nothing.

`shader_dirs` defaults to the game's script directory from the environment. `basegame_dir`
is where the base game's `.pk3` archives live, so the shaders and textures they ship count as
defined; it defaults to the game path joined with the profile's `packaging.basegame`. With a
base game known, `shader_dirs` may be empty: a map that ships no shaders of its own.
shader_audit.signature: (shader_dirs: 'list[str] | None' = None, profile_id: 'str | None' = None, basegame_dir: 'str | None' = None) -> 'dict'

ship_check.doc:
Run the release checklist: naming, levelshot, arena file, package contents.

Conventions come from the profile's `packaging` section, and unverified ones produce
`info` rather than failures — the levelshot size and arena key list are community practice
rather than anything the gamepack documents.
ship_check.signature: (target: 'str | None' = None, profile_id: 'str | None' = None, pk3: 'str | None' = None) -> 'dict'

sightline_report.doc:
Sightline length distribution and power positions.

Samples walkable positions, casts rays between them at the profile's eye height, and reports how
far a player can see. Long uncontested lanes are the finding that matters in a sniper-sensitive
game; "power positions" are the points that see the most of the map.

Sampled, so the numbers move a little between runs. Read the distribution, not any single value.
`detail` as in `balance_report`.

solid_commit.doc:
Compile a Solid IR tree and add the brushes to the open map.

The brushes go to the worldspawn by default. Any other `target_classname` - a door, a
trigger, an objective - makes a new entity of that class on every call, so a second door
is never merged into the first; to add brushes to an entity that already exists, pass its
index as `target_entity`. The result's `entity` says which (`created_entity` when it is
new); give it keys with `entity_set_keys`. `new_entity` is accepted and changes nothing.

`textures` picks shaders per face direction and can make the brushes detail; `solid_help`
lists its keys (`default`, `top`, `bottom`, `north`/`south`/`east`/`west`, `scale`,
`offset`, `rotate`, `detail`).

Nothing is written to disk: call `map_save` for that. The brushes are tagged with a comment
naming `label`, so a human reading the `.map` can see where they came from and delete them
as a unit.

With `remember`, the IR is staged in a `<map>.solids.json` sidecar under `label`, so the
shape can be re-parameterized later with `solid_edit_param` — "make that corridor 32 units
wider" instead of moving faces by hand. The `.map` stays canonical; the sidecar is
advisory and re-derivable.

To commit several solids, use `solids_commit`: one call, all or none.
solid_commit.signature: (ir: 'dict', label: 'str', textures: 'dict | None' = None, grid: 'int | None' = None, target_classname: 'str' = 'worldspawn', remember: 'bool' = True, new_entity: 'bool' = False, target_entity: 'int | None' = None) -> 'dict'

solid_compile.doc:
Compile a Solid IR tree and report what it would produce, touching nothing.

Use this first. It returns brush and face counts, bounds, minimum thickness, off-grid
vertex count and any warnings, so a shape can be checked before it is drawn or committed.

Errors name the failing node by path (e.g. `subtract/cut[0]:box`), because a nested tree is
otherwise very hard to debug from the outside. Call `solid_help` for the operator list.
solid_compile.signature: (ir: 'dict', textures: 'dict | None' = None, grid: 'int | None' = None) -> 'dict'

solid_edit_param.doc:
Change one parameter and replace exactly the solid's unchanged generated brushes.

`solid_param_preview` takes the same arguments and reports the same numbers without
writing; call that first.

Geometry, textures, flags and comments are fingerprinted at creation. If any generated
brush changed manually, replacement is refused. Other brushes and entity keys are kept.
The recorded textures and grid are reused. Map and sidecar stay staged until map_save;
a map checkpoint can undo both together.

solid_help.doc:
The Solid IR reference: every operator, its fields, and the on-grid caveat.

Read this before authoring geometry. It is short.

solid_inspect.doc:
Show a Solid IR tree's structure — either a recorded one by `name`, or one passed in.

The outline names every operator and its parameters with the paths `solid_edit_param`
accepts, which is how you find out what there is to change.

solid_list.doc: Solid IR trees recorded for the open map, with their brush counts.

solid_param_preview.doc:
Show what changing one parameter of a recorded solid *would* produce.

This is the point of keeping the IR: `solid_param_preview("corridor", "max[1]", 192)`
widens a corridor, where editing brushes by hand would mean moving several faces
consistently.

`path` is dotted with bracket indices — `from.solid.max[0]`, `cut[0].min`. Run
`solid_inspect` to see what paths exist.

Nothing is recorded and nothing is drawn. `solid_edit_param` is the one that writes.

solid_preview.doc:
Compile a Solid IR tree and render it **without committing**.

The sculpting loop: author IR, preview, adjust, commit. Nothing touches the open map, so
this is free to call repeatedly.

If a map is open the geometry is previewed in place against it, so a new piece can be seen
in context rather than floating in isolation.
solid_preview.signature: (ir: 'dict', textures: 'dict | None' = None, grid: 'int | None' = None, view: 'str' = 'sheet', width: 'int' = 1100, height: 'int' = 850) -> 'list'

solids_commit.doc:
Commit many Solid IR trees in one call, all or none: crates, pillars, a row of rooms.

Each item is what `solid_commit` takes for one solid: `{"ir": ..., "label": ...}` plus,
optionally, `textures`, `target_classname`, `new_entity` and `target_entity`. The
top-level `textures` applies to every item that gives none of its own.

Items are compiled in order onto a copy of the map, and the copy replaces the map only
if every one succeeds: a refusal names the item (`solids[2] (label 'crate_2'): ...`) and
changes nothing, sidecar included. Labels must be new and distinct. With `remember`, each
tree is staged in the sidecar under its label, so `solid_edit_param` can re-shape any of
them later.

The reply is compact: per item its label, brush count and entity, plus totals, and any
compiler warnings tagged with their label. Nothing reaches disk until `map_save`.
solids_commit.signature: (solids: 'list[dict[str, Any]]', textures: 'dict | None' = None, grid: 'int | None' = None, remember: 'bool' = True) -> 'dict'

spawn_cluster.doc:
Place `count` team spawns where a player can stand, plus the team's spawn-region marker.

`area` is a box `{"min": [x, y, z], "max": [x, y, z]}`: spawns are laid out on a lattice
`spacing` apart (default: the profile's) across its x/y, and stand on floors whose height
lies within its z range. Each position is checked against the map's collision brushes
with the full player box: a floor under it, standing headroom above it, the floor under
the origin within a step (not hanging off a ledge), on the walkable grid, and clear of
existing spawns. When more positions pass than are needed, those nearest the area's
centre are used. If fewer pass, nothing is placed and the reply says why the rest failed.

Every game convention comes from the profile (`spawn_cluster:` in `nrc://profile/{id}`):
the team's spawn classname, the spawnflags for `active` or inactive spawns, the facing key
(`yaw`, degrees), and the marker entity with the team flag and `label` as the name players
pick in the spawn list. `team` is a side's label or name from the profile (ET: red/axis or
blue/allies). `marker=false` adds spawns to a region that already has its marker.

`group` names the cluster so a script can switch it, for a forward spawn: the spawns and
the marker get the names the profile gives, and `group.toggle` in the reply lists the
script actions that switch each (ET: `alertentity <group>` toggles the spawns active,
`alertentity <group>_wobj` swaps the marker's owner). Put them in your own events with
`script_set_event`. One call per group; a name already in use is refused.

All entities are added together or not at all. Nothing reaches disk until `map_save`.
spawn_cluster.signature: (team: 'str', count: 'int', area: 'dict', yaw: 'float' = 0, label: 'str | None' = None, group: 'str | None' = None, active: 'bool' = True, marker: 'bool' = True, spacing: 'float | None' = None, cell: 'float' = 16) -> 'dict'

spawn_safety.doc:
Exits per spawn and distance to the nearest enemy spawn.

A spawn with one exit is a spawn that can be held; a spawn close to an enemy spawn is a spawn
that gets contested immediately. Both are design smells worth seeing before playtesting finds
them. `detail="summary"` (default) lists the riskiest spawns first; `"full"` lists all.

structural_audit.doc:
Find brushes marked structural that need not be — the biggest lever on vis cost.

A structural brush blocks visibility and costs portals; a detail brush does not. Anything not
sealing the map or acting as a major visual blocker should be detail, and converting it is
usually the cheapest large win available on a Q3-engine map.

The estimated benefit per brush is a **heuristic, not a measurement**. The real number needs a
`-vis` compile before and after, which `compile_ab` can do. Treat the list as candidates to
look at, not as a to-do list to apply blindly.

task_list.doc:
Everything this project can do, discovered from mise.

This is the action surface (§1.2). Prefer a task over improvising a shell command: the
task is reproducible by a human and recorded as a name plus arguments. Tasks flagged
`mutates_user_data` need explicit intent before running.

task_run.doc:
Run a mise task by name.

Args:
    name: exact task name from `task_list`.
    args: arguments passed after `--`.
    acknowledge_mutation: required for tasks that mutate user data.

texture_search.doc:
Texture names the base game ships, for brush faces: every server has them, so a map
that uses them packs and draws everywhere.

`query` is matched as space-separated words that must all appear in the name (`floor sand`,
`wall brick`, `trim`); empty lists the texture folders with a count each. Names come back
the way a brush face spells them, without the `textures/` prefix. A name that is not a real
texture packs into a `_FAILEDpack` archive, so pick from here rather than guessing.

Each match says whether a shader script defines it (and its surfaceparms, e.g. `nonsolid`,
`trans`, `nodraw`) or it is a plain image. Shaders whose surfaceparms make them invisible or
non-solid are marked, since they are not wall material.

upstream_diff.doc:
Report upstream drift that would break the editor bridge, against the local baseline.

Hashes the individual declarations in `include/` the plugin binds to, rather than whole files,
so it fires when something the plugin calls has actually moved instead of on every comment
change. Also reports new or removed compiler flags, because each new flag is a potential
optimizer capability.

Reads what is already on disk. `upstream_fetch` is the one that goes to the network.

upstream_fetch.doc:
Fetch upstream and report the drift against what was just fetched.

The same report as `upstream_diff`, but this one **reaches the network** and advances the
stored baseline. Use `upstream_diff` when you only want to re-read what is already here.

validate.doc:
Validate the open map's geometry and file format.

Every finding carries a `rule_source` and a `confidence`. Only `verified` findings are
safe to treat as hard failures.

Scope note: these are the game-agnostic checks — degenerate brushes, duplicate and
mirrored planes, off-grid vertices, thin brushes, patch problems. For the game's own rules
(spawn arrangement, objective counts, gametype keys) call `validate_profile`.

Off-grid and too-thin are errors for geometry added or reshaped since `map_open` - new
work is held to the grid (an angled solid from `solid_commit` cannot be on it; `solid_help`
says which shapes are) - and warnings for brushes the map already had, summarised in one
finding per code: neither stops the compiler or the engine, and an existing map's angled
geometry is not this session's to fix.

validate_profile.doc:
Validate the open map's entities against the active game profile.

Complements `validate`, which covers game-agnostic geometry. This checks the game's own
rules: spawn arrangement, objective counts, gametype keys — and, for a game whose maps
carry a script, that script against the map's entities. For a game with speaker and sound
scripts (the profile's `sound:` section), their syntax, the sound files they name, and
whether the sound scripts and speakers the map and its script name exist. Files are looked
for beside the map (under the folder holding `maps/`) and, with the game path set, in the
base game.

Every rule is data in the profile, and every finding carries a `confidence`. **An
unverified rule can never produce an error** — it is downgraded to `info`;
`nrc://corrections` says why.
